title: Clinical diagnosis and management of spinocerebellar ataxia in a resource-constrained setting: a case report from Eastern Nepal
case_prompt:
A 41-year-old man presented with a 2-year history of insidious, progressive uncoordinated walking and, over the past year, intermittent occipital headache and effortful, unclear speech. He had no history of smoking, alcohol use, toxin exposure, significant past illness, or medication use. He reported that two of his siblings had similar gait problems, whereas his parents and his sister’s children were unaffected.

On examination, he was alert and oriented, with normal vital signs. There was no pallor, icterus, cyanosis, clubbing, lymphadenopathy, or edema. Neurologic examination showed hypotonic limbs with full strength, normal sensation, and intact cranial nerves. Cerebellar signs included scanning speech, horizontal nystagmus, dysmetria on finger-nose testing, dyssynergia on heel-knee testing, dysdiadochokinesia, positive rebound, broad-based gait, and impaired tandem walking. Deep-tendon reflexes were diminished to 1+ in the upper limbs and 2+ in the lower limbs, with pendular responses.

Noncontrast CT of the brain demonstrated marked cerebellar atrophy with prominent folia and widened surrounding cerebrospinal fluid spaces.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Ataxia-telangiectasia was considered but excluded due to absence of characteristic telangiectasia and immunologic features — “The patient did not exhibit the characteristic red ‘spider’ veins or other telangiectatic changes, nor did he report frequent respiratory infections, which are common in AT…”  
2. Friedreich ataxia was considered but excluded based on lack of cardiomyopathy, musculoskeletal abnormalities, sensory loss, and atypical age of onset — “The patient did not show any signs of cardiomyopathy or scoliosis, and sensory functions remained intact… The age of onset for the patient’s symptoms at 41 years is atypical for FA…”  
3. Spinocerebellar ataxia was confirmed by the combination of adult‐onset cerebellar dysfunction, autosomal dominant family history, and CT evidence of cerebellar atrophy — “The diagnosis of spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) was confirmed based on the clinical findings, the patient’s family history and neuroimaging findings.”
